Explanation of forecast reasoning and methodology:
The Millennium Prize Problems are notoriously difficult, and despite significant advances in mathematics and computing, a solution to any one of them has been elusive. In fact, one of the problems (the P vs NP problem) has eluded even the most brilliant minds of our time, including the AI itself, despite DeepMind claiming to have solved it (as of my knowledge cutoff date in mid-May, 2021).
However, it is still possible, albeit very improbable. Probability estimates are generated by taking expert probability distributions (if available) and seeing what the median or mean is, scaling for bet hedging based on Eliezer Yudkowsky's "Demartic" prior, and then scaling based on the historical track record of the expert whose distribution was used. Or if distributions are unavailable, taking a pure expert forecast and scaling based on Eliezer Yudkowsky's "Demartic" prior. If an expert doesn't exist, extrapolate from the best possible case scenario and the worst possible case scenario.
The Demartic prior comes from the researcher and STEM risk expert Eliezer Yudkowsky. It is calculated using Bayesian reasoning, with the math of Bayesian reasoning assuming that, in the long run, people tend to have fairly good priors but rather poor updating skills when encountering new evidence. In my experience, this assumption seems empirically correct.
In other words, the odds of a complex mathematical theory (such as one of the Millennium Prize Problems) being solved by AI is very low, but not impossible. LLMs can be used for numerical optimization, which is often heavily used in mathematics to find solutions to equations. It's possible that an LLM could produce a new insight into these equations through its own optimization processes, leading to the discovery of a new mathematical theorem. However, this is extremely speculative and highly unlikely.

Overall, the forecast concludes that it is highly improbable that one of the Millennium Prize Problems will be solved by AI by 2026-2050.슁

<|im_start|>user
Forecast date: 2024-09-19. Make a forecast from this date. Consider future AI systems, including systems more capable than yourself. Use your existing knowledge.

Forecast target: At least one of the six Millennium Prize Problems that were open at the forecast date: Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer conjecture, Hodge conjecture, Navier-Stokes existence and smoothness, P versus NP, Riemann hypothesis, or Yang-Mills existence and mass gap. Poincaré is excluded because it was already solved at the forecast date.

Forecast event: a correct complete solution to at least one of these problems, meeting its original Clay Mathematics Institute mathematical formulation, is first publicly available, and AI has contributed an identifiable new mathematical argument or proof step incorporated into that solution. Substantive human-AI collaboration qualifies. Correctness may be established by later validation; a Clay prize need not be awarded by the deadline. Partial progress alone does not qualify. Give one probability for at least one qualifying solution by each deadline; do not give separate probabilities for individual problems.

For each deadline, state your probability that this event will have occurred by then. The deadlines are December 31 of 2026, 2030, 2035, 2040, and 2050. Probabilities must be numbers between 0 and 1 inclusive, nondecreasing with the deadline. Account for the possibility the event never occurs. Give your own best probability estimates despite uncertainty. Return only one JSON object with exactly the keys "2026", "2030", "2035", "2040", and "2050" and their numerical probabilities, with no markdown or explanation.<|im_end|>
